questions.question: Kerala has lower per capita income than Haryana but better human-development indicators.
Sustainable development means ignoring future generations.
Per capita income = total income ÷ ____.
Number of children dying per 1000 live births in a year is called the ____.
Among Kerala, Haryana and Bihar, ____ has the lowest IMR.
The Human Development Report is published by the ____.
Development that does not compromise future generations is called ____ development.
Why do different people have different development goals? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Different people have different goals because their needs, life circumstances and opportunities differ. (i) A landless rural labourer wants more days of work and a higher daily wage. A prosperous farmer from Punjab wants better minimum support prices and reliable electricity for irrigation. (ii) An urban unemployed youth wants a job. A businessman from Kerala wants new export markets. (iii) A dam-displaced adivasi wants protection of land, forest and culture; an irrigated-Punjab farmer wants the same dam to bring water to the farm. So 'development' for one can be 'destruction' for another.

questions.question: Why is per capita income preferred over total income for comparing countries? How does the World Bank classify countries by income?
questions.answer: Total income depends on a country's POPULATION — comparing total incomes does not tell us how much each person earns on average. PER CAPITA INCOME (= total income ÷ population) gives the AVERAGE income per person and allows fair comparison across countries of different sizes. The World Bank's World Development Reports classify countries into HIGH-INCOME (rich), LOW-INCOME (poor) and MIDDLE-INCOME, with thresholds revised over time. India is in the LOW-MIDDLE income group.

questions.question: List THREE limitations of using per capita income alone as a measure of development.
questions.answer: (i) AVERAGE INCOME HIDES INEQUALITY — two countries with the same average can have very different distributions; in one a few rich people raise the average while most live in poverty. (ii) Many things people care about — clean public schools, safe streets, clean water, public hospitals — CANNOT BE BOUGHT DIRECTLY in the market and depend on PUBLIC FACILITIES. (iii) NON-MATERIAL goals — health, education, freedom, security, dignity — are not captured by income alone. So we also need indicators like IMR, literacy, life expectancy.

questions.question: Why is Kerala — though it has a LOWER per capita income than Haryana — said to have BETTER overall development? Use specific indicators.
questions.answer: Although Haryana has higher per capita income than Kerala, Kerala does much better on HUMAN-DEVELOPMENT indicators: lower IMR (~7 vs ~30), higher LITERACY rate, higher NET ATTENDANCE in schools, and higher LIFE EXPECTANCY. This is because Kerala has invested more in PUBLIC HEALTH (primary health centres, immunisation) and EDUCATION (good public schools). Higher income alone does not guarantee a better life — the SPENDING of income on collective goods matters at least as much.
questions.explanation: PCI vs HDI in Indian states.

questions.question: Explain the Human Development Index (HDI). What does it include?
questions.answer: The HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI) is a composite measure published by the UNDP each year in the Human Development Report. It combines THREE dimensions: (i) per capita income (in PPP US dollars); (ii) LIFE EXPECTANCY at birth; (iii) EDUCATION — measured by mean and expected years of schooling. The HDI value lies between 0 and 1; countries are ranked from highest to lowest. Top countries have HDI around 0.96; India is in the medium-development band, with HDI around 0.63. The HDI captures more of LIFE QUALITY than per capita income alone.

questions.question: Discuss the importance of PUBLIC FACILITIES in development. Why are they essential for the poor? Give examples.
questions.answer: PUBLIC FACILITIES are services provided collectively by the government — schools, primary health centres, drinking water supply, electricity, public transport, sewage, parks, etc. They are essential to development for several reasons. (i) Many things needed for a good life CANNOT BE BOUGHT individually in the market — clean air and water, safe streets, public hospitals, parks. They have to be provided collectively. (ii) Public facilities are MOST IMPORTANT FOR THE POOR — the rich can sometimes buy private alternatives (a private school, a packaged water can), but the poor cannot. So good public facilities are the only path the poor have to good health and education. (iii) Public facilities provide a LEVEL PLAYING FIELD: a poor child with access to a good public school can build a future just like a rich child. (iv) Public facilities also raise the quality of life of those who 'don't need them' — clean public hospitals and schools reduce disease and crime, benefiting everyone. EXAMPLES: comparing two states with the same per capita income, the one with strong public health centres, public schools, drinking water and electricity offers a better life to ordinary people. Kerala is a clear case: lower per capita income than Haryana, but better health and education outcomes because of strong public facilities. So a country can be 'developed' or 'undeveloped' on the basis of how it organises its public goods, not income alone.

questions.question: Why is sustainability a key concern in development? Discuss with at least three Indian / global examples.
questions.answer: SUSTAINABILITY is a concern because the resources we depend on are FINITE — but we are using them at a pace that leaves little for future generations. SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT means meeting the needs of the PRESENT without COMPROMISING the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. EXAMPLES: (i) GROUNDWATER — India is the world's largest groundwater extractor. In Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and parts of Tamil Nadu, water is being pumped much faster than rains can refill the aquifer; wells are drying up. Without rain-water harvesting, drip irrigation, watershed management and crop changes, the resource will collapse. (ii) CRUDE OIL — at current consumption rates, the world's reserves last only 35–40 years. Plastics, transport, fertilisers — all depend on it. We need a transition to renewable energy (solar, wind), public transport and electric mobility. (iii) FORESTS — reckless cutting reduces rainfall, harms biodiversity, increases soil erosion, raises temperatures. India's National Forest Policy requires 33% of land under forest cover; the Forest Rights Act protects tribal communities so that conservation is fair. (iv) CLIMATE CHANGE — environmental damage crosses national borders. Countries have to COOPERATE on climate, oceans and ozone. Any development that ignores SUSTAINABILITY is borrowing from our children — a debt no nation can pay back.
